## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{17}{17}{17}{17}{16}{16}
\end{marginfigure}

_What is the computer architecture of an autonomous agent?_

A foundation model is not an autonomous computer; it is an unprivileged probabilistic core evaluated on matrix accelerators. Turning continuous token prediction into autonomous agency—sensing, deciding, acting, and learning across extended execution horizons—requires building a complete computing system around the model. Just as the stored-program concept structured deterministic computing into processing, memory, and control, an agentic system requires its own authentic architecture: hierarchical memory to stage working state and durable truth, sandboxed execution to isolate tool actuation under least privilege, supervisory runtimes to manage stateful lifecycles, and verification gates to certify task completion. This textbook establishes the Stochastic Computer as the architectural foundation of autonomous systems, organizing its design around three fundamental exposures: an extended execution horizon, state carried across turns, and authority over external environments.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Contrast the 70-year lineage of agency (cybernetics, symbolic BDI, classical RL) with modern foundation model systems.
- Explain the architectural evolution from static tensors and token serving to stateful, multi-turn trajectories.
- Structure the Stochastic Computer across its four live subsystems (model engine, memory hierarchy, execution sandbox, runtime harness) and supporting fleet infrastructure.
- Apply the principles of least privilege and zero ambient authority to mediate between stochastic token generation and deterministic environments.
- Specify a five-part task contract and apply the Invariant Closure Principle to govern autonomous execution.
- Classify agent workloads across the Horizon, State, and Authority (H·S·A) exposures to determine required systems governance.

:::

## The Agent's Existence Moment {#sec-vol3-intro-existence-moment}

For more than seven decades, the foundational contract of computer systems rested upon the deterministic stored-program concept. As formulated by John von Neumann in 1945 [@vonneumann1945edvac], Alan Turing in his formalization of universal computing machines [@turing1950], and realized on Cambridge's EDSAC by Maurice Wilkes, David Wheeler, and Stanley Gill in 1949 [@wilkes1951preparation], software commanded physical silicon through sequential, explicit machine opcodes. Even when concurrent operating system runtimes, preemptive kernels, and distributed networks contended with asynchronous timing, race conditions, and transient hardware faults, deterministic execution remained the baseline design contract: an instruction pointer advanced deterministically, state transitions followed explicit procedural logic, and non-determinism was an exceptional defect to be isolated and eliminated.

Deep learning fundamentally challenged this paradigm. By substituting hand-engineered procedural algorithms with continuous parameter optimization via stochastic gradient descent [@rumelhart1986], machine learning shifted the computing contract from explicit instructions to learned statistical models. Yet throughout the first decade of deep learning systems—the domain of Volumes I and II of this series—the discipline remained organized around a fundamentally passive abstraction: the **stateless tensor transform** ($X \to Y$). Systems engineering focused on compiling static computational graphs, maximizing General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) efficiency, saturating High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) buses, and scaling distributed training and inference clusters across tens of thousands of accelerators.

Even with the advent of autoregressive foundation models and conversational interfaces, the operational loop remained open. A user submitted a prompt, an inference engine evaluated billions of matrix contractions to sample a sequence of discrete subword tokens, and the server transmitted text over an HTTP socket. The output was conversational advice, code snippets, or analytical summaries. Crucially, the model held zero authority to act upon the world. A human software engineer remained in the loop: reading the proposed code, testing it in a local shell, evaluating side effects, and deciding whether to commit the change. The boundary of machine learning systems ended at the socket buffer.

The **agent's existence moment** occurs the instant we close this loop.

Closing the loop transforms a passive model into an active computing system. Rather than emitting text for human consumption, the system delegates operational authority to the model, directing its emitted token streams into concrete tools, execution sandboxes, and operating system interfaces. The candidate proposal is no longer an inert piece of advice; it is an action intended to mutate an external environment—modifying source code in a repository, running containerized compilers, executing database migrations, or dispatching remote procedure calls across distributed services. The environment executes the mutation, produces physical side effects (standard output, error streams, exit codes, and updated filesystem states), and feeds those observations back into the model's context for the subsequent turn.

This transition from open-loop advice to closed-loop execution is not an incremental optimization. It represents a fundamental discontinuity in systems engineering. The moment execution authority is granted to a non-deterministic, statistical token predictor, every foundational assumption of traditional systems—fault isolation, deterministic state transitions, idempotency, and ambient authority—is overturned.

### The 70-year lineage of agency {#sec-vol3-intro-historical-lineage}

While the integration of foundation models into execution loops appears modern, the conceptual foundation of autonomous agency spans seven decades of computer science and systems theory. Modern agentic machine learning systems represent the convergence of four distinct intellectual traditions:

1. **Cybernetics and Feedback Loops (1940s–1950s):** The foundational mathematics of agency originated in Norbert Wiener's cybernetics [@wiener1960] and W. Ross Ashby's formulation of adaptive homeostasis. Ashby's *Law of Requisite Variety* established that for an agent to regulate a system against external disturbances, the variety of its internal control mechanisms must match or exceed the variety of the disturbances it confronts. Cybernetics treated agency not as symbolic reasoning, but as continuous negative feedback: an agent senses an environmental state, compares it against an equilibrium objective, and applies corrective action to minimize error.
2. **Symbolic Cognitive Architectures and BDI (1970s–1990s):** Early artificial intelligence sought agency through explicit symbolic manipulation and formal logic. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon formulated the *Physical Symbol System Hypothesis* [@newell1976computer], arguing that symbolic manipulation constitutes the necessary and sufficient condition for general intelligent action. This gave rise to the General Problem Solver (GPS), production-rule systems such as SOAR, and the ACT-R cognitive architecture. In distributed systems, this tradition crystallized in the **Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI)** model, which structured software agents around explicit environmental beliefs, motivating desires, and committed plans of intention. While theoretically rigorous, symbolic architectures proved brittle in open domains: they suffered from the *symbol grounding problem*, struggling to map messy, high-dimensional sensory inputs onto rigid symbolic predicates.
3. **Classical Reinforcement Learning (1990s–2010s):** Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto [@sutton2018reinforcement] formalized agency within the mathematical framework of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Here, an agent is an active policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ interacting with an environment $\mathcal{E}$, receiving scalar reward signals $r_t$, and updating its parameters via dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning. Classical reinforcement learning provided a rigorous foundation for optimal control, credit assignment, and exploration-versus-exploitation trade-offs. However, it was historically bounded by state-space tractability: scaling classical RL to open-ended software tasks was bottlenecked by sparse rewards, sample inefficiency, and the difficulty of formalizing arbitrary software engineering workflows as compact reward functions.
4. **The Foundation Agent Convergence (2020s):** The contemporary breakthrough occurred when autoregressive foundation models were placed directly into closed control loops, as demonstrated by ReAct [@yao2023react] and Reflexion [@shinn2023reflexion]. By training on web-scale text, code repositories, and technical documentation, foundation models acquired broad world knowledge, code generation capabilities, and linguistic common sense. Crucially, they resolved the symbol grounding problem by adopting natural language and source code as the universal interface for reasoning, planning, and tool interaction.

### The systems paradox of modern agency {#sec-vol3-intro-systems-paradox}
[]{#sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible}
[]{#sec-vol3-intro-operational-incident}

The convergence of foundation models and closed-loop control resolves the historic bottlenecks of symbolic planning and sample-inefficient reinforcement learning. Yet it introduces a profound systems paradox:

> *We have solved the symbol grounding problem by adopting an unprivileged probabilistic core that possesses zero ambient authority, exhibits non-deterministic execution paths, and fails plausibly.*

An autoregressive language model evaluated in isolation cannot complete an operational task. Evaluated on a cluster of matrix accelerators, the neural core is a purely mathematical function: it takes an assembled token buffer, evaluates floating-point tensor contractions across billions of parameters, and emits a probability distribution over vocabulary tokens. It cannot open a TCP socket, cannot read a file descriptor, cannot execute a POSIX system call, and cannot verify whether its proposed mutation satisfied the underlying task contract.

If a host script naively takes the model's raw emitted text and pipes it directly into an unconfined shell (`subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True)`), any hallucinated command line flag, syntax error, or prompt injection executes with the full privileges of the host process. Conversely, if a command fails, the model has no native mechanism to roll back destructive mutations, isolate contaminated state, or verify semantic correctness. As Edsger Dijkstra observed, testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence; an unprivileged neural core can neither detect its own silent regressions nor certify task completion without external software oracles.

Agency is not an intrinsic property of the foundation model. Rather, **agency is an architectural property of the complete computer system**.

To transform a statistical token generator into a dependable, recoverable, and autonomous computing machine requires building an authentic systems architecture around it. That complete machine is the **Stochastic Computer**.

## From Tensors to Trajectories {#sec-vol3-intro-evolution-of-ml-systems}

Machine learning systems have evolved across three distinct architectural epochs: single-node static tensor graphs, distributed token-serving clusters, and stateful multi-turn trajectories. With each transition, the fundamental unit of systems management has expanded from fixed algebraic operations to open-ended operational lifecycles, ultimately stretching execution time across thirteen orders of temporal magnitude. Systems engineers can no longer treat the machine learning runtime as a passive, stateless function evaluator. Engineering autonomous systems requires building an active, stateful host supervisor capable of managing extended execution horizons, isolating irreversible environmental side effects, and enforcing correctness across non-deterministic computational paths.

### The three epochs of machine learning systems {#sec-vol3-intro-three-epochs}

The systems challenges of modern artificial intelligence reflect a historical shift in the fundamental unit of execution that the runtime must schedule, allocate memory for, and protect. Systems engineers have navigated two foundational transitions over the past two decades, and are now engaged in a third. As mapped in @fig-vol3-three-epochs, machine learning infrastructure has evolved across three architectural epochs, each defined by distinct execution units, memory models, control flows, and hardware bottlenecks:

1. *Era 1 (Static Tensors):* The execution unit is an immutable directed acyclic graph ($X \to Y$) with statically pre-allocated accelerator memory buffers, compute-bound dense GEMM kernels, and deterministic execution bounded to milliseconds on single nodes.
2. *Era 2 (Distributed Tokens):* The execution unit shifts to an iterative token sequence ($t_k$), where dynamic autoregression decouples prompt lengths from output lengths, requiring dynamic PagedAttention Key-Value (KV) caches across distributed clusters, bounded by high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth.
3. *Era 3 (Closed-Loop Trajectories):* The execution unit expands into an open-ended multi-turn trajectory loop ($\tau$), interleaving stochastic model calls with deterministic tool RPCs, isolated sandbox execution, and out-of-band verifiers across hours of wall-clock time.

::: {#fig-vol3-three-epochs fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Three Epochs of Machine Learning Systems Execution**: Historical evolution of machine learning systems units from static, compile-time tensor computation graphs to decoupled token-serving loops and stateful, multi-turn agentic trajectories. Each successive epoch expands the systems management boundary across orders of magnitude in execution time, shifting optimization from dense accelerator kernel arithmetic to durable host-side state and invariant verification." fig-alt="Systems diagram comparing the three epochs of machine learning systems across four architectural rows: execution unit, memory model, control flow, and physical substrate. Era 1 features static tensor graphs with pre-allocated device buffers on single accelerators. Era 2 features autoregressive token sequences with dynamic PagedAttention KV caches across distributed serving clusters. Era 3 features stateful closed-loop trajectories with four-tier tiered memory hierarchies spanning host supervisors, sandboxes, and foundation model inference clusters."}
![](images/svg/three_epochs_execution_units.svg)
:::

The first epoch centered on **Single-Node Tensors and Static Graphs**. In this regime, typified by early multilayer perceptrons, deep convolutional networks, and fixed-length sequence-to-sequence encoders, the primary workload consisted of deterministic feedforward passes over static multidimensional arrays. The compiler constructed an immutable directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tensor operations prior to execution. Memory management was predominantly static: frameworks allocated physical device memory at initialization, avoiding runtime heap churn through pre-computed buffer reuse. Execution was compute-bound, dominated by large, dense General Matrix Multiplications (GEMMs) and convolutions where arithmetic intensity was high enough to saturate floating-point hardware units. The systems boundary began and ended within a single accelerator or a tightly coupled multi-GPU node executing synchronized data-parallel steps. The duration of an invocation was strictly bounded: a forward pass through a deep residual network took tens of milliseconds and consumed an invariant number of arithmetic operations.

::: {.column-margin}
**Trajectory ($\tau$):** An ordered sequence of interleaved state representations, candidate actions, external tool observations, and verifier verdicts:
$$\tau = (s_0, a_0, o_1, s_1, a_1, o_2, \dots, s_T)$$
representing the complete lifecycle of a delegated task across an unprivileged foundation engine and its supervising host environment.
:::

The second epoch emerged with the rise of autoregressive foundation models, marking the transition to **Distributed Tokens and Dynamic Attention**. Here, the fundamental unit of execution shifted from a static tensor graph to an iterative token-generation loop. The Transformer architecture decoupled input length from output length, introducing dynamic execution paths governed by data-dependent stopping criteria. Systems engineers were suddenly confronted with two radically distinct computational phases within a single request: a compute-bound prompt prefill phase dominated by parallel General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) operations, followed by an autoregressive token decode phase dominated by memory-bandwidth-bound General Matrix-Vector (GEMV) operations.

During prompt prefill, the engine processes context in parallel via compute-bound General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM), reusing parameter weights across all tokens in the sequence to saturate accelerator arithmetic units. In contrast, sequential token decoding operates via memory-bandwidth-bound General Matrix-Vector (GEMV). For autonomous agents, this distinction carries a critical systems implication: at batch size $B=1$ (the operational reality of an interactive agent loop awaiting tool feedback), token decoding is physically bounded by memory bandwidth because the entire parameter matrix must be shuttled from memory for each emitted token. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model provides the canonical derivation of the Roofline model, arithmetic intensity, and accelerator hardware balance from first principles.

### Temporal stretching across thirteen orders of magnitude {#sec-vol3-intro-temporal-stretching}
[]{#sec-vol3-intro-duration-accounting}

The transition from isolated model calls to stateful trajectories represents an unprecedented expansion in the time horizon that a systems runtime must manage. As illustrated in @fig-vol3-evolution-execution-units, the basic unit of computational scheduling has expanded across thirteen orders of temporal magnitude over the past seven decades: from hardware instruction cycles executed by microprocessors in sub-nanoseconds ($10^{-9}\text{ s}$), through subroutines ($10^{-6}\text{ s}$), operating system processes ($10^{-3}\text{ s}$), distributed RPCs ($10^0\text{ s}$), and container workflows ($10^2\text{ s}$), to multi-turn autonomous trajectories ($10^3 - 10^4\text{ s}$).

::: {#fig-vol3-evolution-execution-units fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Temporal Progression of Systems Execution Units**: Systems abstraction layers and execution timescales spanning thirteen orders of temporal magnitude, from sub-nanosecond hardware opcodes to kilosecond autonomous agent trajectories. Managing long-horizon trajectories forces the host runtime to incorporate transactional durability, memory compaction, and non-blocking asynchronous tool mediation." fig-alt="Logarithmic time scale ladder diagram illustrating the evolution of computer system execution units across thirteen orders of magnitude. The scale spans from nanosecond hardware instructions at 10 to the minus 9 seconds, microsecond subroutines at 10 to the minus 6 seconds, millisecond POSIX processes at 10 to the minus 3 seconds, second-scale distributed RPCs at 10 to the 0 seconds, minute-scale container workflows at 10 to the 2 seconds, to multi-hour autonomous trajectories at 10 to the 3 and 10 to the 4 seconds."}
![](images/svg/evolution_execution_units_v2.svg)
:::

Each historical step up this temporal ladder demanded new systems primitives. Subroutines required hardware call stacks and activation records. Multi-tasking operating systems required virtual memory page tables, timer interrupts, and kernel protection rings. Distributed services required remote procedure calls, distributed consensus, and idempotent retry envelopes.

At the trajectory scale ($10^3 - 10^4\text{ s}$), classical operating system primitives are necessary but insufficient. When an autonomous agent attempts an engineering task—such as diagnosing a regression in a distributed codebase, writing a patch, and running integration test suites—the execution spans hundreds of distinct tool invocations across dozens of minutes. Over such an extended horizon, systems will inevitably experience transient network disconnects, tool sandboxes will exhaust memory quotas, external APIs will rate-limit requests, and the neural engine will occasionally emit invalid tool syntax.

A runtime that treats an agent trajectory as a monolithic, uninterrupted sequence of execution will inevitably fail. Managing extended horizons demands that the runtime supervisor treat the trajectory as a stateful, recoverable computation: checkpointing intermediate state to a Write-Ahead Log (WAL), enforcing resource quotas, and coordinating compensating transactions when tools partially fail.

### The passive request boundary {#sec-vol3-intro-passive-boundary-ceiling}

Why do the serving systems designed for Era 2 fail when applied directly to autonomous agents? The bottleneck lies in the **passive request boundary**.

In conventional machine learning infrastructure, model serving is structured around an RPC interface modeled after stateless microservices. A client submits a payload containing a prompt. The serving cluster schedules the request, streams tokens back across an HTTP connection, and immediately drops all session activations from high-bandwidth device memory once the connection terminates. The serving engine operates entirely open-loop: it possesses no native actuation mechanisms, cannot execute an operating system process, cannot inspect a filesystem diff, and cannot verify whether its generated code compiles.

When human engineers interact with conversational chatbots, the human provides the missing closed-loop controller, as illustrated in @fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control. If a model generates code containing a syntax error, the human copies the compiler trace back into the prompt. The human manages the context, executes tools in their local terminal, inspects error logs, and decides when the task is complete.

::: {#fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Open-Loop Serving versus Closed-Loop Agent Supervision**: Structural comparison between conversational model serving and autonomous agent supervisory control loops. While traditional inference relies on human operators to manually interpret advice and test code changes, autonomous agent architectures delegate closed-loop supervision to a deterministic host runtime that isolates tool execution and programmatically evaluates verification oracles." fig-alt="Architectural comparison diagram between open-loop serving and closed-loop agent supervision. In the upper panel representing Era 2, a client sends an input prompt to an inference cluster, which returns tokens to a human operator who manually runs code in a terminal and pastes back error traces. In the lower panel representing Era 3, a host runtime supervisor programmatically maintains context memory, intercepts unprivileged model proposals, executes tools in an isolated sandbox, and routes structured observations and verifier evidence back into context."}
![](images/svg/open_vs_closed_loop_control.svg)
:::

Autonomous agency replaces this manual human loop with software. However, delegating the supervisory role to software immediately exposes two severe systems bottlenecks:

1. **Context Memory Bloat and Stranding:** Unlike conversational chats that discard state after every turn, an agentic trajectory accumulates working history across dozens of turns. Staging raw tool outputs, compiler dumps, and file diffs inflates the prompt to tens of thousands of tokens, triggering quadratic attention overhead during prefill and consuming gigabytes of accelerator memory. Furthermore, when an agent dispatches a long-running tool—such as a 60-second test suite—holding the agent's Key-Value cache in accelerator High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) strands expensive GPU memory while drawing idle power.
2. **The Verification Deficit:** A foundation model possesses no native ground truth. It cannot determine whether an operation succeeded; it can only predict the most statistically probable continuation of its context. If an agent modifies a database or alters a configuration file, the model will readily generate fluent, authoritative explanations asserting that the task succeeded even when the underlying system has completely collapsed.

These bottlenecks cannot be resolved by training larger foundation models or tweaking prompt instructions. They require an authentic computer architecture that decouples memory management from accelerator hardware, sandboxes tool execution under least privilege, and verifies task invariants through independent, deterministic software oracles.

## The Anatomy of the Stochastic Computer {#sec-vol3-intro-stochastic-computer}

Wiring an autoregressive language model directly to an operating system shell produces an immediate architectural breakdown: the neural model executes purely as a stateless matrix accelerator routine that cannot hold operating system file descriptors, cannot dispatch hardware interrupts, and cannot verify whether its proposed mutation completed successfully or corrupted the host environment. When a host script naively feeds raw model-generated token strings to `exec()` or `subprocess.Popen()`, any hallucinated flag, malformed syntax, or adversarial injection executes with the full privileges of the user account. The resulting construct possesses neither memory virtualization nor fault isolation. If the stochastic policy emits a catastrophic mutation or loops indefinitely, the underlying host platform has no native mechanism to roll back side effects, reclaim unindexed context, or certify invariant satisfaction.

::: {.column-margin}
In 1945, John von Neumann formulated the classical stored-program architecture in *First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC*, partitioning the computer into a Central Arithmetic part (CA), a Central Control part (CC), Memory (M), Input (I), and Output (O). In von Neumann's design, CC held absolute authority to sequentially fetch, decode, and execute instructions loaded into memory. An agentic system inverts this relationship: the neural engine is an unprivileged arithmetic core stripped of all ambient authority, while CC is replaced by an external, deterministic host runtime.
:::

**The Stochastic Computer is a software-level functional architecture in which learned computation, state, controlled interaction, and supervision form the live loop, while training and fleet operations improve and operate it across tasks.** Rather than casting the foundation model as an autonomous CPU,[^fn-stochastic-computer-karpathy] the architecture treats it as an unprivileged, non-deterministic inference engine that holds zero ambient authority. The model evaluates context and proposes candidate actions, but all state evolution, memory assembly, tool dispatch, and invariant verification are mediated by deterministic software layers executing on general-purpose host processors. At a 30,000-foot view, the blueprint maps how the parts of an agentic system fit together: the foundation model provides learned computation (analogous to a statistical processor core), context buffers and durable stores manage memory, execution sandboxes provide controlled input and output, the agent runtime acts as the supervisory control plane, trajectory post-training recompiles behavior from verified traces, and distributed fleet infrastructure scales the machine across concurrent tasks.

[^fn-stochastic-computer-karpathy]: **The Stochastic Computer vs. Classical Von Neumann Architecture**: Karpathy popularized an intuitive mental model likening large language models to operating systems in late 2023, comparing the neural network to a central processor (CPU), context windows to RAM, and tools to peripheral devices. However, treating this metaphor as a literal systems design guide creates fundamental engineering failures. A CPU is a deterministic instruction execution unit with hardware privilege rings, interrupt lines, and memory protection units; an LLM is an unprivileged, stochastic floating-point inference engine bounded by memory bandwidth ($B_{\text{mem}}$) and arithmetic intensity ($I$), completely lacking execution authority, hardware interrupt dispatch, or memory virtualization. The Stochastic Computer formalizes the true systems architecture: an unprivileged inference engine running under zero ambient authority, wrapped within a deterministic host runtime harness that manages physical memory hierarchies, sandboxed actuation, and invariant verification. \index{Karpathy, Andrej!LLM OS critique}\index{Stochastic Computer!architectural definition}

### The live execution loop: Four functional subsystems {#sec-vol3-intro-live-loop}
[]{#sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle}

The operational core of an agentic system is the live execution loop, which drives the closed-loop state transitions formalizing task execution over a trajectory $\tau = (s_0, a_0, o_1, s_1, \dots, s_T)$. This loop is not a monolithic program, but the coordinated interaction of four distinct functional subsystems, each operating within strict trust and authority boundaries:

1. **The Foundation Model Engine:** Represents the unprivileged learned computation of the system. Its sole physical responsibility is to ingest an assembled context buffer $c_t \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{tok}}^*$ and compute the conditional probability distribution over vocabulary tokens to emit a candidate proposal $a_{\text{prop}} \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid c_t)$. The engine executes atop specialized matrix accelerators configured for high-throughput tensor contractions. Crucially, the foundation model engine has no direct access to host storage, sockets, or operating system primitives; it cannot evaluate whether its emitted tokens constitute valid shell syntax, nor can it grant itself permission to execute them. It is a pure computational predictor.
2. **The Context Memory Hierarchy:** Governs the storage, indexing, and eviction of the system's working set. Because physical accelerator memory is severely constrained by hardware bandwidth and capacity, the memory subsystem decouples the active context window from durable system state. At the lowest layer sits the volatile Key-Value (KV) cache, storing precomputed attention states in high-bandwidth accelerator memory for immediate token generation. Above the KV cache lies the structured context staging buffer, managed by the host runtime, which dynamically synthesizes task definitions, system instructions, retrieval augmentations, and historical trajectory checkpoints into the token sequence $c_t$. Durable memories—such as episodic task logs, semantic vector indexes, and external relational databases—are decoupled from accelerator memory and accessed exclusively through explicit query interfaces.
3. **The Execution Sandbox:** Implements the principle of least privilege through mediated tool actuation. The sandbox serves as the physical airlock between the stochastic proposals of the model engine and the external environment $\mathcal{E}_{\text{env}}$. When the runtime receives a candidate action $a_{\text{prop}}$, it deserializes the proposal into a typed remote procedure call (RPC) and validates it against security constraints and capabilities. Permitted actions $a_{\text{perm}}$ execute within hermetic, disposable virtualization boundaries—such as Linux containers, microVMs, or restricted system namespaces. The sandbox captures raw outputs, exit codes, and hardware telemetry, transforming them into a structured observation tuple $o_{t+1} = (\text{stdout}, \text{stderr}, \text{exit\_code})$ before passing them back to the supervisor.
[]{#sec-vol3-intro-prompt-injection}
4. **The Agent Runtime Harness:** The supervisory control plane that governs the lifecycle of the entire machine. The runtime maintains the authoritative system state $\mathcal{S}_{\text{sys}}$, orchestrates context assembly, dispatches actions to the sandbox, and evaluates invariant closures $\mathcal{I}(s_t, v)$. It manages the fault-tolerance infrastructure of the agent, maintaining a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) to record state transitions before execution and coordinating compensating transactions (Sagas) when a tool invocation fails. The runtime enforces Dijkstra's verification principle: it never queries the foundation model to determine whether a task is complete, but instead evaluates external, deterministic test suites, compilers, and static analyzers to establish verifiable truth.

The unified functional architecture of the Stochastic Computer is presented in @fig-vol3-agentic-architecture, bridging live task execution with across-task fleet infrastructure:

::: {#fig-vol3-agentic-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Functional Architecture of the Stochastic Computer**: System architecture blueprint decomposing an agentic platform into a live execution loop and across-task fleet infrastructure. The live loop couples an unprivileged foundation model engine, context memory hierarchy, isolated execution sandbox, and host agent runtime supervisor. The across-task infrastructure coordinates trajectory harvesting, offline policy optimization, and distributed fleet scheduling. This architectural partitioning ensures that stochastic inference operates under zero ambient authority while the host runtime enforces memory paging, tool containment, and invariant verification." fig-alt="Comprehensive systems architecture diagram of an agentic platform. The central live execution loop depicts the interactions among the Foundation Model Engine, Context Memory Hierarchy, Execution Sandbox, and Agent Runtime Supervisor under zero ambient authority. Surrounding the live loop is the across-task fleet infrastructure, showing trajectory harvesting into persistent event stores, policy compilation via fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and distributed fleet operations managing multi-tenant scheduling and telemetry."}
![](images/svg/agentic_systems_architecture.svg)
:::

|:-----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| **Foundation Model Engine**  | Autoregressive token sequence and candidate action proposal generation | Matrix accelerator cluster (GPU/TPU) running inference kernels | Assembled context sequence $c_t \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{tok}}^*$      | Raw candidate proposal token stream $a_{\text{prop}}$   | Constrained decoding grammars and JSON schema validators |
